title: Method of determining loosely bound compounds of heavy metals in the soil
author: Minkina, Mandzhieva, et al.

steps.title: Air‑dry and sieve soil
steps.instruction: Air‑dry soil samples in a room at 20–24 °C and 60–70 % relative humidity until moisture is ≤5–6 % (dry to the touch). Remove large particles and plant residues, grind the soil with a pestle and mortar, then sieve through a 1 mm sieve (Russian standard; 0.25 mm may also be used).

steps.title: Prepare ammonium acetate buffer
steps.instruction: To make 1 L of 1 N ammonium acetate buffer (pH 4.8 for neutral/alkaline soils, pH 4.5 for acidic soils), add 108 mL of 98 % glacial acetic acid and 75 mL of 25 % NH₄OH to 600–800 mL distilled water, allow the solution to cool if it heats up, measure pH with an ionometer and adjust with additional acetic acid or NH₄OH as needed, then bring the volume to exactly 1 L with distilled water and mix thoroughly.

steps.title: Prepare 1 % EDTA solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve 10 g of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) in 1 L of the 1 N ammonium acetate buffer prepared above to obtain a 1 % (w/v) EDTA solution.

steps.title: Prepare 1 N HCl solution
steps.instruction: Add 82 mL concentrated HCl to 500–600 mL distilled water, allow the mixture to cool if it heats up, then bring the volume to 1 L with distilled water and mix.

steps.title: Extract loosely bound metals
steps.instruction: Perform parallel extractions on each soil sample:

substeps.instruction: Weigh 5.0 g of the prepared soil into a conical flask (minimum three analytical replicates per sample).
Add 50 mL of ammonium acetate buffer (pH 4.8) to the flask, agitate continuously for 3 min.
Add 50 mL of the 1 % EDTA solution to a second flask containing the same amount of soil, agitate for 3 min.
Add 50 mL of 1 N HCl to a third flask with the same soil, agitate for 3 min.
Allow each flask to stand for 18 h at room temperature.
After 18 h, agitate each extract for an additional 3 min before filtration.

steps.title: Filter extracts and store
steps.instruction: Filter each extract through appropriate filter paper, then transfer the filtrate to a closed glass jar and store at 4 °C until analysis.

steps.title: Analyze extracts by atomic absorption
steps.instruction: Measure Pb, Cu and Zn concentrations in the extracts using a KVANT 2‑AT atomic absorption spectrophotometer (Kortec Ltd, Russia).

substeps.instruction: Calibrate the instrument with standard solutions.
Set the wavelengths to 283 nm for Pb, 325 nm for Cu, and 213.7 nm for Zn.
If an extract’s concentration exceeds the calibration range, dilute the extract 10‑fold with distilled water before measurement.

steps.title: Determine total metals by XRF
steps.instruction: Determine total heavy‑metal content in the original soil by X‑ray fluorescence (XRF) using a MAX‑GV spectroscan (SPECTRON, Russia).

substeps.instruction: Analyze each sample in bulk mode for 45 s per sample.
No digestion is required; the method detects up to 26 elements simultaneously.

steps.title: Run blanks, controls and replicates
steps.instruction: Prepare blank and control samples alongside the extracts, perform blank‑correction, and carry out all laboratory tests in triplicate.

steps.title: Optional: Prepare contaminated soil incubation
steps.instruction: If validation with spiked soils is required, set up a one‑year incubation as follows:

substeps.instruction: Collect soil from the 0–20 cm layer at the monitoring site; mix five initial samples to obtain a composite sample for each soil type (Chernozem Haplic, Chernozem Calcic, Kastanozem Haplic).
Sieve the composite soil through a 2 mm sieve.
Place a 3 cm layer of washed glass beads at the bottom of each 2 L plastic vessel with a closed drainage system.
Add 1 kg of the sieved soil to each vessel.
Spike the soil with dry copper, zinc and lead acetates to achieve target addition rates of 55, 100, 300, 1000 or 2000 mg kg⁻¹, according to the experimental design.
Incubate the vessels at room temperature under normal lighting for one year.
After incubation, proceed with the soil preparation, extraction and analysis steps described above.

description: For an objective assessment of the degree of environmental pollution, it is necessary to study not only the total content of pollutants in soil but also their loosely bound compounds. The diversity of the heavy metal compounds in soils makes it practically impossible and unfeasible to determine all the individual metal-bearing substances that are present in the particular soils. It is more efficient to determine the groups of heavy metal compounds differing in their mobility (migration capacity) in the given soils. The analysis of the metal group composition in the soil allows one to reveal the genetic specificity of the particular soils and to trace the effects of different factors on the soil properties. The main goal of the suggested method is the determination of the mobility of heavy metals in soils based on the data of their distribution between two major groups: firmly bound and loosely bound with the soil components. A group is a totality of metal compounds similar in binding strength to soil components and, hence, in migratory capacity and biological availability. The group of firmly bound compounds includes the metals strongly fixed in the structures of primary and secondary silicate and nonsilicate minerals, as well as the metals in difficultly soluble compounds and stable organic and organomineral compounds. The group of loosely bound compounds includes the metals associated with the soil particle surface with the organic and mineral soil components in the exchangeable and specifically sorbed states. Loosely bound compounds are the most important group of metals for the ecological point of view, as it enters plants and dispersed to environments. Hazardous ecological consequences of soil contamination with metals are related to these compounds [[1], [2], [3]].
